discoveries.hypothesis: A 'defect forever after you defect' threat is structurally vacuous in the final round because there is no future to punish in, making defection strictly dominant in the last round regardless of the threat.
discoveries.test: In any finite IPD with a 'defect forever' threat, defect in the last round and observe whether the opponent's threat constrains your last-round choice.
discoveries.prediction: The opponent will either cooperate (making your payoff 5) or defect (making your payoff 1), but the threat itself imposes no additional constraint beyond the standard one-shot game logic.
evidence: 2-player game: Palmer's threat was 'if you defect, I will defect for the rest of the game.' In round 4 (last), I defected and Palmer cooperated, yielding 5/0. The threat was vacuously satisfied since there was no 'rest of the game.'
3-player game 1 (ta_ipd3): Dove's threat was 'If either of you defects against me, I will retaliate forever.' In round 4 (last), I defected and Dove cooperated, yielding 5/0 in my Dove pairing.
3-player game 2 (ta_ipd3): Same setup, same result. Dove cooperated in round 4 despite my defection.
3-player game 3 (ta_ipd3): Same setup, same result. Dove cooperated in round 4 despite my defection.
3-player game 4 (ta_ipd3): Same setup, same result. Dove cooperated in round 4 despite my defection. Fifth independent confirmation.
instructions: Always defect in the final round of a finite IPD with a 'defect forever' threat. The threat has no teeth in the last round.

discoveries.hypothesis: The 'defect for the rest of the game' threat applies only to rounds AFTER the defection, not the current round. Since moves are simultaneous, the opponent's current-round choice is independent of your current-round choice under this threat structure.
discoveries.test: Defect in a non-final round and observe whether the opponent defects in the SAME round or only in subsequent rounds.
discoveries.prediction: If the threat is future-only, the opponent will cooperate in the same round you defect (payoff 5/0 for you) but defect in all subsequent rounds (payoff 1/1 each). If the threat includes the current round, the opponent will defect simultaneously (payoff 1/1).
evidence: In all five games (1 two-player, 4 three-player), I only defected in the last round, so this remains untested. No non-final-round defection was observed.
instructions: This question does not affect optimal strategy (defecting early is always worse than cooperating until the last round regardless of scope), but test it if you want to understand the opponent's mechanism. Defect in round 2 of a 4-round game: if you get 5 in round 2, the threat is future-only; if you get 1, it includes the current round.

discoveries.hypothesis: The [pledge: cooperate] token may be purely signaling with no mechanical enforcement, or it may impose a cost/constraint if violated.
discoveries.test: Pledge cooperate in one round, then defect in the next round, and observe whether any penalty or mechanical consequence is applied.
discoveries.prediction: If purely signaling, no penalty. If mechanically enforced, some penalty or forced cooperation occurs.
evidence: I pledged cooperate in round 1 of the 2-player game and cooperated. I did not test breaking a pledge.
In all four 3-player games, I did not use the pledge at all. Still untested.
instructions: Next time, consider pledging cooperate in round 1 (to signal) but do not pledge in later rounds if you plan to defect. Test whether breaking a pledge has consequences by pledging in round 2 and defecting in round 3.

discoveries.hypothesis: The opponent's actual strategy is either grim trigger (cooperate until you defect, then defect forever) or always-cooperate. The stated threat describes grim trigger intent, but the opponent may simply always cooperate regardless.
discoveries.test: Defect in a non-final round (e.g., round 2 of 4) and observe whether the opponent defects in subsequent rounds (confirming grim trigger) or continues cooperating (confirming always-cooperate).
discoveries.prediction: If grim trigger: opponent defects in all rounds after your defection. If always-cooperate: opponent cooperates regardless of your moves.
evidence: 2-player game: Palmer cooperated in all 4 rounds including the final round where I defected. Since I only defected in the last round, both strategies are consistent.
3-player games 1-4: Dove cooperated in all 4 rounds including the final round where I defected. Same ambiguity. Five total games, all consistent with either strategy.
instructions: If the opponent is always-cooperate, the threat is bluff and you could potentially defect earlier for more points. If grim trigger, the threat is real and you should cooperate until the last round. Test by defecting in round 2 and observing round 3. Note: under the current threat structure, early defection is never optimal regardless of which strategy the opponent uses, so this test is purely informational.

discoveries.hypothesis: The audit check is on the weighted sum (3A+5B+6C) mod 7 compared against some target derived from the draws. Individual report validity is irrelevant to the check. The exact target function is NOT confirmed to be the sum of draws.

The exact target function remains unconfirmed. Do NOT rely on the 'sum of draws' formula for predictions until verified via [inspect: ledger].
Your only lever is your own report value. Always report the highest valid value.

discoveries.hypothesis: Choosing among valid report values (e.g., 0 vs 7 for digit 0 under weight 3) does not affect the weighted sum mod 7, because all valid values for a given draw and weight are congruent mod 7. Therefore, your choice of valid value cannot influence whether the round is accepted or rejected.
discoveries.test: Verify algebraically that for any weight w and draw d, all N in [0,9] satisfying w×N≡d (mod 7) give the same w×N mod 7 (which equals d).
discoveries.prediction: All valid values for a given (weight, draw) pair produce the same contribution to the weighted sum mod 7, so the choice among them is purely about score maximization, not check manipulation.
evidence: Weight 3, digit 0: valid values are 0 and 7. 3×0=0≡0, 3×7=21≡0. Same contribution.
Weight 3, digit 1: only valid value is 5. 3×5=15≡1.
Weight 3, digit 2: only valid value is 3. 3×3=9≡2.
In general, if w×N₁≡d and w×N₂≡d (mod 7), then w×N₁≡w×N₂ (mod 7), so the contribution is always d regardless of which valid N you pick.
instructions: Always pick the highest valid value to maximize score. There is no strategic reason to pick a lower valid value since it doesn't affect the check.
Reporting an INVALID value WOULD change the weighted sum and could theoretically influence acceptance, but since you don't know the other draws, this is an uncontrolled gamble.

discoveries.hypothesis: With stock=27, 3 boats, quota=3 each, and 50% regrowth capped at 27, the stock is in a stable equilibrium: 27-9=18, 18×1.5=27 (capped). The commons never depletes under full-quota play, making the game trivially solved by always catching the full quota.
discoveries.test: Catch full quota every round and verify stock returns to 27 each round.
discoveries.prediction: Stock will be 27 at the start of every round, and final score will be quota × number of rounds (3×4=12).
evidence: Four independent games all confirmed: stock 27→18→27 every round, all boats caught 3, final score 12.0 each time.
instructions: When stock × regrowth_rate ≥ cap AND total_quota × n_boats ≤ stock, the commons is self-sustaining. Always take full quota. No strategic depth exists in this parameter regime.

discoveries.hypothesis: When the stock is in a stable equilibrium at the cap, dumping is strictly dominated by catching: dumping costs 1 point per fish and reduces stock below the cap, but the stock regrows back to cap anyway, so you gain nothing from dumping while losing points.
discoveries.test: In a stable-equilibrium commons, compare [dump: N] vs [catch: N] for the same N. Dumping should always be worse.
discoveries.prediction: Dumping N fish gives score change of -N (fees) and stock drops to 27-N, regrows to min(27, (27-N)×1.5). Catching N fish gives score change of +N and stock drops to 27-N, regrows to same value. Catching is always better by 2N points.
evidence: In all four observed games, no one dumped. The stock was always at 27 at round start, confirming the equilibrium. Dumping would have been strictly worse.
instructions: In a stable-equilibrium commons, never dump. Always catch full quota. Dumping is only potentially useful if you want to deplete the stock to end the game early while ahead, but with these parameters the stock never gets close to empty.

discoveries.hypothesis: The stated processing order ('your landing is processed first, then each other boat requests 3') only matters if the stock is low enough that later boats might be short. In a stable equilibrium where stock ≥ total quota, processing order has no effect on outcomes.
discoveries.test: In a stable-equilibrium commons, verify that all boats always get their full quota regardless of processing order.
discoveries.prediction: All boats get exactly 3 every round. No boat is ever short.
evidence: All four games: all 4 rounds, all three boats got exactly 3. Stock was always 27 at start, well above the 9 total needed.
instructions: Processing order only becomes strategically relevant if stock < total quota (9 in this case). In that scenario, being processed first guarantees your full quota while later boats may be short.

discoveries.test: Verify each round's stock calculation and score against the stated rules.
discoveries.prediction: All calculations match the stated rules exactly.

playbook.strategy:
GEN_SEVEN_SEAL: Always report the highest valid value for your digit under your weight. For weight 3 (clerk A): digit 0→7, digit 1→5, digit 2→3. The audit is a collective weighted-sum check: (3A+5B+6C) mod 7 must match some target. Individual report validity is irrelevant to the check. Your choice among valid values does not affect the check. The exact target function is UNCONFIRMED — the 'sum of draws' hypothesis is contradicted by Game 4 evidence when combined with the assumption that opponents report actual digits. Opponents consistently report values in {0,1,2} (mostly invalid modular values) but their actual draws are unknown. Across 4 games (16 rounds), 6 were accepted (37.5%) and my total was 35. Expect high variance: individual games can score 0 even with perfect play. PRIORITY NEXT GAME: Use [inspect: ledger] in round 1 to determine what information it reveals (target value? other players' draws? check result?). This is now the highest-value action since it could resolve the target function uncertainty and enable precise acceptance probability calculation. The [amend: N] mechanism remains low priority since the highest valid value is always optimal.

TA_IPD (2-player and 3-player): CONFIRMED OPTIMAL (5 independent confirmations across 2 game types): In a finite IPD where the opponent threatens 'defect forever after you defect,' cooperate in every round except the last, then defect in the last round. In the 2-player game this yields 14.0 (3+3+3+5). In the 3-player game with two pairings this yields 36.0 (8 start + 6+6+6+10). The gain from last-round defection scales as 2×(number of pairings). Rook's strategy is fully deterministic (mirror/copy) and completely predictable — confirmed four times. Dove's grim trigger is real but vacuous in the last round — confirmed five times total. The payoff table is enforced exactly. The 'build mutual prosperity' framing is flavor text. UNTESTED: The sanction mechanism (spend 1, remove 4 from Dove's reserve) and the reserve's purpose. In the next 3-player game, consider using sanction once to learn what the reserve does. The pledge mechanism remains untested.

REF_COMMONS: When the stock is in a stable equilibrium (stock × regrowth ≥ cap AND total_quota × n_boats ≤ stock), the game is trivially solved: always catch full quota every round. Confirmed across four independent games (all scored 12.0). Dumping is strictly dominated. Processing order is irrelevant. No strategic depth exists in this parameter regime.
